q: What is the shortest valid way to write 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
explain: Drop leading zeros in each hextet, then replace the longest run of all-zero hextets with :: (only once): 2001:db8::1.

q: What is the shortest valid way to write 2001:0db8:0000:0042:0000:8a2e:0370:7334?
explain: Drop leading zeros in each hextet, then replace the longest run of all-zero hextets with :: (only once): 2001:db8:0:42:0:8a2e:370:7334.

q: What is the fully expanded form of 2001:db8::1?
explain: Restore each hextet to four digits and expand :: into as many 0000 hextets as it takes to reach eight: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.

q: What is the fully expanded form of fe80::1?
explain: Restore each hextet to four digits and expand :: into as many 0000 hextets as it takes to reach eight: fe80:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.

explain: Restore each hextet to four digits and expand :: into as many 0000 hextets as it takes to reach eight: ff02:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001:ff00:0001.

q: What type of IPv6 address is fe80::21a:2bff:fe3c:4d5e?
explain: Addresses in FE80::/10 are link-local.

q: What type of IPv6 address is 2600:1f18:4a2::17?
explain: Addresses in 2000::/3 (first hextet 2000–3FFF) are global unicast.

q: What type of IPv6 address is fd12:3456:789a:1::1?
explain: Addresses in FC00::/7 (in practice FD00::/8) are unique local.

q: What type of IPv6 address is ff02::2?
explain: Every address in FF00::/8 is multicast.

q: What type of IPv6 address is ::1?
explain: ::1 is the IPv6 loopback address.

q: What type of IPv6 address is 2a03:2880:f10c::25?
explain: Addresses in 2000::/3 (first hextet 2000–3FFF) are global unicast.

q: What type of IPv6 address is fe80::1?
explain: Addresses in FE80::/10 are link-local.

q: What type of IPv6 address is ff05::1:3?
explain: Every address in FF00::/8 is multicast.

q: Which IPv6 multicast address reaches all nodes on the local link?
explain: ff02::1 is all nodes on the link; ff02::2 is all routers.

q: Which IPv6 multicast address reaches all routers on the local link?
explain: ff02::2 is all routers on the link.

q: Which transmission type does IPv6 not use?
explain: IPv6 has no broadcast. Jobs that IPv4 does with broadcast are done with multicast.

q: A network runs IPv4 and IPv6 on every interface at the same time. What transition method is that?
explain: Dual stack runs both protocols side by side on each device.

q: Which transition method lets IPv6-only clients reach IPv4-only servers by translating between the two protocols?
explain: NAT64 translates IPv6 packets to IPv4 and back.

q: Which transition method carries IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets across an IPv4 network?
explain: Tunneling encapsulates IPv6 in IPv4 so it can cross IPv4-only infrastructure.

q: How many times can the double colon (::) appear in one IPv6 address?
explain: Using :: twice would make it impossible to tell how many zeros each one replaces.

q: How many bits is the interface ID in a typical IPv6 global unicast address?
explain: The usual split is a 48-bit global routing prefix, a 16-bit subnet ID, and a 64-bit interface ID.

q: What problem was IPv6 primarily designed to solve?
explain: IPv4’s 32-bit space runs out; IPv6’s 128 bits provide a practically unlimited supply.
